Linear Regression · Regression03

Where "Regression" Comes From

In 1886 Francis Galton compared the heights of 928 adult children with the heights of their parents (205 families).

Tall parents had tall children, but the children were usually closer to average than their parents, and the same was true for short parents. Galton called this "regression towards mediocrity".

The line he drew through the data kept the name, which is why fitting a line is called linear regression even when nothing is regressing.

The Simplest Model: A Line

Linear Regression · Regression05

Linear Regression

Unfortunately, because linear regression is so old, it has a lot of vocab specific to it that has accrued and changed over time, depending on the field using it. This can make it tricky to recognize a linear regression in different contexts.

\lk{yhat}{\yhat} = \lk{slope}{\omega_1 x_1} + \lk{w0}{\omega_0}
  • ŷ: the prediction (predicted target)
  • ω1, ω0: slope and intercept
  • x1: the input feature

Ordinary Least Squares

ℒ(\omega) = \norm{y - X \omega\T}^2 \text{take the gradient and set it to } 0 -2\,X\T (y - X \omega\T) = 0 \text{multiply out} \lk{normal}{X\T X\,\omega\T = X\T y} \text{multiply both sides by } (X\T X)^{-1} \omega\T = \lk{xtx}{(X\T X)^{-1}} \lk{xty}{X\T y}

Linear Regression · Fitting the line16

Give X a column of 1s for the intercept, then follow the OLS recipe.

X\T = \Bb{\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \end{matrix}} \qquad y\T = \bb{\begin{matrix} 14 & 20 & 31 & 40 & 49 \end{matrix}} X\T X = \Bb{\begin{matrix} 5 & 20 \\ 20 & 90 \end{matrix}} \qquad X\T y = \Bb{\begin{matrix} 154 \\ 706 \end{matrix}} (X\T X)^{-1} = \frac{1}{50}\Bb{\begin{matrix} 90 & -20 \\ -20 & 5 \end{matrix}} \omega\T = \frac{1}{50}\Bb{\begin{matrix} 90\cdot154 - 20\cdot706 \\ -20\cdot154 + 5\cdot706 \end{matrix}} = \Bb{\begin{matrix} -5.2 \\ 9.0 \end{matrix}}

So ŷ = 9.0 x1 − 5.2: about 9 points per 100 yards.

Linear Regression · Fitting the line17

What the Line Learned

Quick check: in 2018 Notre Dame gained 550 yards against Stanford. What does this line predict, and what is the residual if Notre Dame scored 38?
x1 = 5.5, so ŷ = 9.0 × 5.5 − 6.7 = 42.8 points. The residual is y − ŷ = 38 − 42.8 = −4.8: Notre Dame scored about 5 points fewer than its yards suggest.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
games = pd.read_csv("nd_football.csv")
X = games[["nd_total_yards"]] / 100 # hundreds
y = games["nd_points"]
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
print(model.coef_.round(2), model.intercept_.round(2))
print(round(model.score(X, y), 2)) # R²

Linear Regression · Fitting the line19

Multiple Linear Regression

When we perform a linear regression on a dataset with more than one feature, we call this a multiple linear regression.

Hyperplanes

With one feature the model is a line, with two it's a plane and with more than two it's a hyperplane.

Quick check (old exam question): what would the equation look like for a multiple linear regression with three features?
ŷ = ω1 x1 + ω2 x2 + ω3 x3 + ω0: one weight per feature, plus the intercept.

Representing Curves

Not every dataset is best represented with a straight line. How could you use a linear regression to model a sine wave?

A linear regression is only linear in its weights, not in its inputs.

\yhat = \omega_0 + \omega_1 x + \omega_2 \sin(1.25x)

The Bias-Variance Tradeoff

The bias–variance tradeoff describes the relationship between a model's complexity, the accuracy of its predictions (measured as overall error), and how well it can make predictions on unseen data.
